I'm Irawati, and Asif sits beside me in second-year economics. After the winter break he was gone for almost six weeks, in and out of hospital with an illness nobody in class really understood. When he came back he was thinner and slower on the stairs.
In the canteen, one of the boys said, loud enough, "That's what happens if you live on hostel junk food and never sleep." Someone else added, "We get what we earn, na." People laughed.
Asif didn't laugh. He picked up his tray and left. After that he stopped answering in class, even when the professor asked him directly. I can't say what he was thinking. But he used to argue about everything, and now he just writes, head down.

qa.q: How long was Asif gone after the winter break?
qa.a: He was gone for almost six weeks.

qa.q: What might Asif's silence in class suggest, even though Irawati can't be sure?
qa.a: It may suggest he felt ashamed and hurt, as if the illness were his own fault, so staying quiet felt safer than drawing attention.

qa.q: Irawati has noticed the change in Asif. What choice could Irawati make now?
qa.a: Irawati could sit with Asif, say the canteen jokes were unfair, and offer notes from the weeks he missed, making it easier for him to speak again.

qa.q: How might the boy who joked about junk food see his comment, compared with how Asif hears it?
qa.a: To him it may be a throwaway line that makes illness seem like something careful people avoid; to Asif it turns being sick into a personal failing.

grounding: A classmate watches a male student go silent after others imply his illness was his own fault.

Monday: Result day. Nikhil had failed two papers in his second year. He had studied, but weeks of night shifts at his uncle's shop had eaten his sleep. He told himself he'd explain at home.
Saturday: At the family lunch, Payal Bua heard the news before he could say anything. "Failing doesn't come from nowhere, beta. You must have been wasting time with friends." Heads nodded around the table. Nikhil opened his mouth, then shut it and passed the dal.
The next Friday: Vandana, his lab partner, messaged: "Want to prep together for the re-exam?" He typed "I'm fine," deleted it, and sent nothing. He hadn't told anyone about the shop, and now it felt too late.

qa.q: What did Payal Bua say about why Nikhil failed?
qa.a: She said, "Failing doesn't come from nowhere, beta. You must have been wasting time with friends."

qa.q: Why did Nikhil shut his mouth at the family lunch instead of explaining?
qa.a: With heads nodding at Payal Bua's verdict, mentioning the night shifts might sound like an excuse, so shame made silence feel safer.

qa.q: When Vandana's message arrived, what choice could have turned things around for Nikhil?
qa.a: Replying yes, and telling even one person like Vandana about the shop shifts, could break the silence and get him real help for the re-exam.

qa.q: What would change if Payal Bua had asked 'What happened?' instead of assuming?
qa.a: Nikhil would have had room to mention the night shifts, and the family might have helped with his sleep and study instead of adding shame.

grounding: A male student who fails two papers hears relatives say he must have deserved it, and slips into silence.

passage:
Kalyani, sit. Let me tell you something your Mama never told anyone.
When I was nineteen, in college in Kolkata, I got jaundice in my final year and missed my exams. Everyone had an opinion. The neighbour aunty said, "Arnab must have been eating from roadside stalls, what did he expect?" A professor told me, in front of the class, that "discipline shows in the body." My own cousins joked that I was being taught humility.
I was already weak and yellow and frightened. After that, I also felt dirty, as if I had done something wrong. So I stopped talking about it. For a whole year I told people I had "taken a break by choice."
That's why, when you told me about your friend's illness yesterday, I didn't ask what she did wrong.

qa.q: What illness did Arnab get in his final year?
qa.a: Arnab got jaundice in his final year.

qa.q: Why did Arnab tell people he had 'taken a break by choice'?
qa.a: The blame made him feel dirty and ashamed, as if the illness were his fault, so hiding the truth felt easier than hearing more judgement.

qa.q: What choice did Arnab make when Kalyani told him about a friend's illness, and why does it matter?
qa.a: He chose not to ask what the friend did wrong, so Kalyani sees illness met with support rather than blame.

qa.q: How might Kalyani see her uncle differently after hearing this story?
qa.a: Kalyani may see that even a strong elder was once silenced by shame, which could make it easier for Kalyani to speak openly about hard things.

grounding: An uncle recalls how blame after his student illness added shame and made him hide it for a year.

It was the week before semester exams, and the hostel power kept cutting out, so Yash was studying by his phone torch when the anonymous memes started again. Someone in the seniors' group was editing his photo onto cartoons, mocking his accent. It had been going on for a month.
When he mentioned it to a batchmate, the answer came fast: "You must have annoyed them somehow. They don't pick on random people."
Yash went quiet. Maybe it was his fault. Maybe his accent was the problem. He stopped going to the mess and stopped replying in groups.
Aadhya, from his lab batch, noticed he had skipped three meals. She sat beside him on the stairs. "It's not your fault," she said. "Nobody deserves that."
That afternoon she walked with him to the college counsellor. The counsellor listened, told Yash plainly that none of it was his fault, and contacted the anti-ragging committee the same day.

qa.q: What was being mocked in the memes?
qa.a: His accent was being mocked, with his photo edited onto cartoons.

qa.q: Why did Yash stop going to the mess and replying in groups?
qa.a: After being told he must have annoyed them, he began to feel ashamed, wondering if it was his fault, so he withdrew into silence.

qa.q: What turning point helped Yash, and why did it matter?
qa.a: Aadhya told him it was not his fault and walked him to the counsellor, who listened, said so plainly, and contacted the anti-ragging committee the same day.

qa.q: What would change for Yash if people had only kept saying he must have annoyed the seniors?
qa.a: He might have stayed silent and alone, carrying shame on top of the hurt, while the harassment continued unchecked.

grounding: It shows a student being harassed and told he must have provoked it, which adds shame and silence, until a friend and counsellor reject that blame.

passage:
At a cousin's wedding in a Pune banquet hall, Dhruv, twenty, sat at the edge of the relatives' table in a kurta that hung loose after two months in bed with a long illness. He had lost a semester.
Manoj Mama leaned across the gulab jamuns. "At your age, illness doesn't come from nowhere. Late nights, outside food, isn't it? You must have done something."
A few aunties nodded. Someone added, "Everything happens for a reason."
Dhruv's face went hot. He had eaten at home, slept early, done everything right. But he said nothing. He looked at his plate until the music started, then went and stood by the parking lot.
His mother found him there. "It wasn't your fault," she said quietly. "Mama doesn't know." Dhruv nodded but didn't answer. On the drive home he kept the window down, letting the noise of the road fill the silence.

qa.q: How long had Dhruv been in bed with the illness?
qa.a: Two months in bed with a long illness.

qa.q: Why did Dhruv say nothing to Manoj Mama?
qa.a: Being told he must have done something made him feel ashamed, even though he had done everything right, so he went quiet instead of defending himself.

qa.q: What did Dhruv's mother do that could help him, and why?
qa.a: She went to find him and told him quietly that it wasn't his fault, which counters the shame the relatives' words added.

qa.q: How might Manoj Mama see his own comment?
qa.a: Manoj Mama probably thinks he is being wise or caring, not realising that his words add shame to Dhruv's pain and push him into silence.

grounding: It shows a student who suffered a long illness being told he must have caused it, which adds shame and silences him.

College counsellor's note, 7 February
Sachin, second year, came in today, brought by his friend Siddharth. He was in hospital with typhoid for three weeks in December and missed his exams. Since coming back, he says, people keep telling him it was his own fault: an uncle said he "must have eaten rubbish from street carts," and a classmate said "weak people fall sick." He has started skipping lunch in the canteen so nobody comments, and he stopped answering the class group. He said, "Maybe they're right. Maybe I did something." I told him clearly that illness is not a punishment and that he did nothing to deserve it. We made a plan for the supplementary exams together, and I will write to his department about extra time. Siddharth will walk with him to the canteen tomorrow.

qa.q: How long was Sachin in hospital?
qa.a: Three weeks in December.

qa.q: Why has Sachin started skipping lunch in the canteen?
qa.a: He feels ashamed and hurt after being told his illness was his own fault, so avoiding people feels safer than hearing more blame.

qa.q: What did the counsellor do, and why does it help?
qa.a: Told Sachin clearly that illness is not a punishment, planned his supplementary exams and asked for extra time, easing both the shame and the practical problem.

qa.q: How might Siddharth feel walking with Sachin to the canteen?
qa.a: Siddharth probably feels protective and caring, wanting Sachin to feel less alone.

grounding: A counsellor records a student who, after a long illness, is told he must have deserved it and falls silent in shame.

passage:
Monday night
Results came. Failed thermodynamics. I knew it might happen; my father was in hospital for most of October, and I was at his bedside instead of in class.
But nobody asks about that. My hostel senior said, "Should have studied instead of roaming." A relative on the phone told Amma I must have been "wasting time with friends." Even the professor said, "You get what you work for." Each time I just nodded. What do you even say?
Now I feel like maybe I am lazy. I haven't told anyone how much it hurts.
Tanvir knocked tonight and asked if I'd eaten. I said yes. I hadn't.
Tomorrow maybe I'll tell Tanvir about October.
Tarun

qa.q: Where was Tarun for most of October?
qa.a: At the father's bedside in hospital, instead of in class.

qa.q: How is Tarun feeling after the comments?
qa.a: Tarun feels hurt and ashamed, starting to believe the lazy label, and has told no one how much it hurts.

qa.q: What could help Tarun now?
qa.a: Telling Tanvir, the professor or a counsellor about October, so people understand the real reason and the re-exam can be planned with support.

qa.q: Why might Tanvir have knocked to ask if Tarun had eaten?
qa.a: Tanvir probably noticed Tarun was upset and wanted to check on Tarun gently.

You asked why I skipped the results party, Pema. Okay. I'm Francis, and I failed Thermodynamics. First time in my life I've failed anything.
The first thing my uncle said on the phone was, "You must have been roaming with friends." Then a senior in the mess: "Bhai, the paper was easy, you didn't study." Then my own roommate, joking: "God is fair, man."
I studied. I had solved every past paper. I blanked on two questions and misread a third. That happens. But when four people in a row tell you it's your fault, you start walking differently. I stopped going to the mess at lunch. I took the stairs so I wouldn't meet anyone in the lift.
Last night I told my professor all of it, and she said, "Failing one paper doesn't make you lazy. It makes you a student." That's the first sentence in weeks that let me breathe.

qa.a: Francis failed Thermodynamics.

qa.q: What was Francis feeling after so many people blamed the result on laziness?
qa.a: Francis felt ashamed and exposed, and began avoiding the mess and the lift to escape more blame.

qa.q: Which response helped Francis, and why?
qa.a: The professor's line that failing one paper makes you a student, not lazy, separated the result from Francis's worth and finally let Francis breathe.

qa.q: How might the roommate see the joke about God being fair?
qa.a: The roommate probably meant it as light teasing, without noticing how it added to Francis's shame.

grounding: Shows a student who failed an exam hearing people say he deserved it, which adds shame and makes him withdraw.

Chetan blinked. Nobody had said it wasn't his fault. They went together after class.
